items.question: What problem does method overloading solve?
items.answer: Answer: Without method overloading, similar operations may require different method names such as: addOne() addTwo() addThree() When many methods perform the same task with different inputs, remembering every method name becomes difficult. Method overloading allows all such methods to use one meaningful name, such as add().

items.question: What is method overloading?
What conditions allow methods to have the same name?
items.answer: Answer: Methods can have the same name when at least one of the following is different: Number of parameters Types of parameters Order of parameter types These differences create distinct method signatures.

items.question: How is method overloading achieved by changing the number of parameters?
How is method overloading achieved by changing parameter types?
How is method overloading achieved by changing parameter order?
Can parameter names differentiate overloaded methods?
Can methods be overloaded only by changing the return type?
Why does the return type not participate in method overloading?
items.answer: Answer: Java selects an overloaded method using the method name and arguments supplied during the call. The compiler checks: Number of parameters Parameter types Parameter order The return type alone cannot identify which method should execute.

items.question: Are these methods valid overloads?
Are these methods valid overloads?
What is a duplicate-method error?
items.answer: Answer: A duplicate-method error occurs when a class contains methods with: The same method name The same number of parameters The same parameter types The same parameter order Changing only the parameter names or return type does not prevent this error.

items.question: What is a method signature in method overloading?
items.answer: Answer: For method overloading, the method signature is identified using: Method name Number of parameters Types of parameters Order of parameter types Example: add(int, float) is different from: add(float, int)

items.question: How does Java select an overloaded method?
items.answer:
Answer: Java examines the arguments supplied during the method call and selects the method whose parameter signature matches those arguments. Example:

```java
add(10, 20);
```

This matches: add(int, int) because integer literals are treated as int by default.

items.question: Which overloaded method executes for add(10, 20)?
Which overloaded method executes for two float arguments?
Which overloaded method executes for two double arguments?
Can the return value of an overloaded method be printed directly?
items.answer:
Answer: Yes.

```java
System.out.println(add(10, 20));
```

The method executes first, and its returned value is passed directly to println(). A separate result variable is not compulsory.

What is a multiline comment in Java?
items.answer:
Answer: A multiline comment begins with /* and ends with */.

```java
/*
```

This is a multiline comment. These lines will not be executed.

```java
*/
```

It is used to comment out a block of multiple lines.

items.question: What is the difference between single-line and multiline comments?
items.answer:
Answer: A single-line comment uses //:

```java
// This is a single-line comment
```

A multiline comment uses /* and */:

```java
/*
```

This is a multiline comment

```java
*/
```

Single-line comments affect one line, while multiline comments affect the complete enclosed block.

items.question: What is polymorphism?
items.answer: Answer: Polymorphism is the process of a single entity taking multiple forms. The word can be divided as: poly means many morph means forms Therefore, polymorphism means one entity appearing or behaving in multiple forms.

items.question: How is method overloading connected to polymorphism?
items.answer: Answer: In method overloading, one common method name appears in multiple forms. For example: add(int, int) add(float, float) add(double, double) add(int, int, int) The method name is the same, but each method has a different parameter signature.

items.question: What is virtual polymorphism?
items.answer: Answer: Virtual polymorphism is an appearance that one entity is taking multiple forms. In method overloading, the user sees one common method name performing different operations based on the supplied arguments. However, separate method definitions handle the different argument combinations.

items.question: What is overloaded in method overloading?
items.answer: Answer: Nothing is literally overloaded. Multiple separate methods share the same name. This creates the appearance that one method is performing multiple tasks. Each overloaded method performs one specific task based on its parameter signature.

items.question: Write a program demonstrating all three rules of method overloading.
What are the important interview rules for method overloading?
items.answer: Answer: Multiple methods can have the same name. Their parameter signatures must differ. The number of parameters may differ. The parameter types may differ. The order of parameter types may differ. Changing parameter names does not create overloading. Changing only the return type does not create overloading. Methods with identical parameter signatures are duplicates. Java selects the method by matching the supplied arguments. Method overloading provides one common name for similar operations.
